stem.text: Which row gives the 5th to 14th ionisation energies for phosphorus?

explanation.text: Phosphorus is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>: five electrons in the third shell, eight in the second and two in the first. Successive ionisation energies rise steadily within a shell and jump sharply each time the next electron has to come from a shell closer to the nucleus, because that electron is much less shielded and much nearer the nucleus.

So the 5th ionisation energy is still a third-shell electron (no big jump yet), the 6th to 13th are the eight second-shell electrons (a big jump at the 6th, then a steady rise), and the 14th is the first electron from the first shell (a second, much bigger jump).

optionAnalysis.text: The small rise from 6270 to 8410 for the 6th would mean a sixth electron in the third shell; phosphorus has only five outer electrons, so the big jump must come at the 6th.

Correct. The 5th (6270) is the last third-shell electron, there is a large jump at the 6th (21 270), eight second-shell values from 6th to 13th, then a huge jump at the 14th (271 800) for the first 1s electron.
Places the huge jump at the 13th, which would leave only seven electrons in the second shell instead of eight.
Places the first large jump at the 5th, which would mean only four outer electrons (a Group 14 element), not five for phosphorus.

reasoningChain: Write the configuration of P: 2, 8, 5 electrons in shells 1, 2, 3.
Electrons 1–5 come from shell 3, so the 5th should continue the gradual rise (about 6000).
Electrons 6–13 come from shell 2, so expect a large jump at the 6th, then eight gradually increasing values.
Electron 14 comes from shell 1, so expect a very large jump at the 14th.
Only row B has big jumps exactly between the 5th and 6th and between the 13th and 14th.

inferredMistakes.text: Counting the electrons in each shell wrongly (for example treating P as having four outer electrons) and putting the first big jump in the wrong place.
Looking only at whether values increase, which all four rows do, instead of locating where the large jumps fall.
